*See also: [How to do it](eportfolio-guide.qmd) · [Criteria](eportfolio-criteria.qmd) · [Checklist](eportfolio-checklist.qmd) · [An IB example](eportfolio-example.qmd)*

Every year the IB writes a subject report on what examiners saw. These are the problems from the **May 2026** report that
matter for music, roughly in order of how many marks they cost.

## 1. Going over 30 pages

**The problem:** portfolios longer than 30 pages (or the equivalent in minutes). Anything past the limit "cannot be
considered for assessment". If Task 1 alone runs over, Tasks 2, 3 and 4 are not marked at all. "Several students presented
highly accomplished final artworks that could not be considered due to excessive page count or video/audio duration."

**Instead:** keep a running total in the [page budget](eportfolio-checklist.qmd#page-budget). Remember that one minute of
audio or video is two pages, that everything but the bibliography counts, and that a video of the song you critique counts
too. Shrinking the font or speeding up a recording to fit is not allowed.

## 2. A topic that is not a genre or movement

**The problem:** "some students did not select topics or techniques that could be considered movements or genres of
Music." A single song, one artist, or a technique is not a genre.

**Instead:** name a genre or movement (punk, protest folk, reggae, Nueva canción, conscious hip-hop) and write about it as a
whole: where it came from, what it stands for, what it sounds like across several recordings. Artists are part of it, but
"not all of this".

## 3. Critiquing the lyrics instead of the music

**The problem:** "students often critiqued song lyrics rather than the music in order to meet the requirements for strand
Aii."

**Weaker:** *"The lyrics say the government is lying, which shows the song questions power."*

**Stronger:** *"At 1:12 the band drops out and the last line is sung over one held chord, so the accusation lands with
nothing to soften it."* The lyric is still there, but the critique is about what the **music** does with it.

## 4. Elements and techniques, but hardly any context

**The problem:** "Even when techniques and elements were addressed in detail, students could not achieve higher levels when
the context was barely mentioned."

**Instead:** give context real space in both Ai and Aii, and explain how it **shaped the music**, not just when it was
released.

## 5. Screenshots instead of sound in Bi

**The problem:** "In Music, screenshots of computer music programs continue to be submitted as evidence instead of drafts of
compositions or audio and video excerpts of work in progress." Also: lots of writing with few trials, voice-overs drowning
the music, sped-up clips, and a camera that cuts off the player.

**Instead:** record at the beginning, the middle and towards the end. Keep clips short, at normal speed, with no talking
over them, and write your commentary beside them. A DAW screenshot can sit next to the audio of that draft, never instead
of it.

## 6. Writing about the process in Di

**The problem:** "students still struggled to critique their own artwork and wrote about the process of their work rather
than appraising it."

**Instead:** in Di, judge the **finished recording**: strengths and limitations of its elements and techniques, with time
stamps, measured against your artistic intention. The story of how you made it belongs in Bi and Dii.

## 7. Mixing up Di and Dii

**The problem:** the hardest strand. Students "often failed to make the crucial distinction between analysing an artwork and
analysing themselves as developing artists", commenting on outcomes and "failing to identify key learning moments, evolving
intentions, or the influences shaping their practice."

**Instead:** Dii is about **you as a musician**. What can you do now that you could not in week 1? Which moment changed your
approach? Who influenced you? Point to the Bi clip that shows each change.

## 8. Links, unreadable pages, and missing citations

**The problem:** "hyperlinks are not accessible by examiners", "Examiners will not zoom in to read small font sizes", and
"There are still instances when students submit work that is not appropriately cited."

**Instead:** upload every file; normal font size; cite every source in the text and the bibliography.

## 9. Letting AI make the music

**The problem:** "Care however must be taken not to rely on AI to compose music for students." AI can help with
brainstorming and planning, "it should not be used to create the whole artwork".

**Instead:** the music must be yours. If you used an AI tool at any stage, say what for and cite it.
